data.title: Component
data.tagline: A component is a unit that groups a reusable piece of interface with the behavior it owns.
data.learningOutcome: You can identify an interface area that should change together and distinguish it from a whole-page layout or one-off content.
data.description: For example, a product card can be shared by the home page, search results, and saved items when all show an image, price, and purchase action. An input field can also be a component. Components divide interface responsibility; not every tiny label needs to become one.

learning.assumes: You have seen the same kind of card or button appear in several places on one site.
learning.outcome: You can identify an interface area that should change together and distinguish it from a whole-page layout or one-off content.

distinctions.label: State
distinctions.explanation: A Component defines one piece of UI structure and responsibility. State records changing information such as whether that component is open or saving.

explanation.title: Keep repeated responsibility together
explanation.text: A card's structure, styles, and click behavior can be maintained together, so a price format or button-label change does not require edits on three pages.

explanation.title: Pages compose components
explanation.text: A page arranges navigation, cards, and filters for its current task. The same component can receive different product data while retaining consistent interaction and appearance.

explanation.title: Control what components display with parameters
explanation.text: Components accept parameters (called Props in React) to control what they display. For example, a product card component receives product name, price, and image from the outside. When you tell AI "make this component accept a title parameter", you're describing Props.

data.boundary: A component is not exclusive to a framework, nor is it another word for a whole page. React, Vue, and plain web pages can all use components. One-off plain text with no independent responsibility does not need forced extraction.

lessonPractice.title: The event page, homepage, and search page all need cards with the same rules. Which approach makes later changes consistent?

options.label: Put the image, title, state, and click behavior in one event-card component, with each page passing its own data
options.feedback: Correct. The card's shared responsibility lives in one place, so a style or behavior change reaches all three pages.

options.label: Copy the card code into every page, then edit titles and buttons separately
options.feedback: It can show content initially, but shared rules become scattered and will drift or be missed later.

options.label: Put every page and feature into one component named Website
options.feedback: That does not separate responsibilities. A component should make one reasonably independent part of the interface easier to understand and maintain.

data.agentPrompt: Turn the repeated event card into a component. Use it on the home, event, and search pages while keeping each page's image, title, and state as inputs. Afterward, check that the card looks and behaves consistently on all three pages.
